messages.subject: The sparse parametrisation of the BYM-model
parts:
Dear INLA users,

I have a question that might be a bit technical. Any help would be appreciated.  

I have read the paper An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling. 

I do not quite follow on the sparse-ness property of the BYM-model, which is derived in the paper. In the paper it is stated that the precision matrix of [w1,w2] is


Q_tot=
[ tau/(1-phi) I-matrix,-sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix   ]
[ -sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix, Q_*+phi/(1-phi) I-matrix    ]

where I is an identity-matrix.

If we invert  Q_tot and then consider the lower right block of this matrix, i.e. the covariance matrix for the spatial term, (call it Sigma22) and then invert this, we get Sigma_22^{-1}=Q_*, which is sparse. But have we not enforced a sum to zero constraint on w_2? Then the precision matrix should not be sparse? We should have that Sigma_22 = Q^(-1)-Q^(-1)t(A)((AQ^(-1)t(A)))^(-1)AQ^(-1)   (Taken from Rues book). 

I have tried to illustrate the calculations using the Germany-dataset and the example used in the help-section for the function  inla.scale.model.

Where am I wrong?

#Example start

#Small number to be added to the diagonal of Q

eps = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)

library(INLA)

data(Germany)

g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")

source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))

 

 

Q = -inla.graph2matrix(g)

diag(Q) = 0

diag(Q) = -rowSums(Q)

n = dim(Q)[1]

Q.scaled = inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n), e=0))

Q.scaled

Q.scaled.eps=Q.scaled+diag(n)*eps

 

A=matrix(1, 1, n) 

tau_b=0.5

phi=0.5

I=Matrix(0,n,n,sparse=TRUE)

diag(I)=1

upper=cbind(tau_b/(1-phi)*I,-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I)

lower=cbind(-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I,Q.scaled.eps+phi/(1-phi)*I)

Precision=rbind(upper,lower)

Sigma=solve(Precision)



#Extract the covariance matrix for the spatial term

Sigma.spatial=Sigma[(n+1):(2*n),(n+1):(2*n)]


diag(Q.scaled.eps)-diag(solve(Sigma.spatial))

#The diagonals match


solve(Sigma.spatial)

#Which is sparse,


 #We see that the elements are the same.  One example:

Q.scaled.eps[544,534]

solve(Sigma.spatial)[544,534]


#However, is w2~sim N(0,Q.scaled.eps^-1) or N(0,Q.scaled^-) where Q.scaled^- is #the generalized variance.

 

#What is the sigma of the spatial term under sum to zero constraint? Expression from Rue's book.

A=matrix(1, 1, n)

Component1=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps))

Component2=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A)%*%solve(A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A))%*%A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps))

Sigma.spatial.correct=Component1-Component2

diag(Sigma.spatial.correct)-diag(solve(Q.scaled.eps))

#These do not match, as expected.


#Example end 

Best regards

Fredrik

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] The sparse parametrisation of the BYM-model
parts:
Yes, I believe that is correct. INLA uses 'conditioning by Kriging' to correct for the constraints while retaining the sparsity of the Q matrix. See section 2.3.3 of Rue and Held (and eqn 2.31 for how to efficiently calculate the conditional density, which I glossed over too quickly on my first **several** reads...).

Thanks,
Jeff

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] The sparse parametrisation of the BYM-model
parts:
Hi,

thanks for pointing to the note, I had forgot about that one. That is my
notes for that model (and the computations of the pc-prior).

This way of writing it, on page 3, will preserve sparsity.

the sum-to-zero constraint, is imposed, as Jeff said, afterwards, by
doing a rank one correction (also to the density) as described in the
GMRF book. (the ``conditioning by Kriging'' stuff, but using Bayes
formula for the density)

Best
H

On Mon, 2020-07-27 at 04:12 -0700, FredrikLAa wrote:
> Thanks again for your comments.
>
> If this is correct, then sparseness is not preserved? I thought
> conditionining by krigning was used on samples, ie. you sample from
> the uncondtional model and then "correct" this sampe to have the
> correct distribution.
>
> Should not eq. 2.31 b used in the calculations? It seems like only
> pi(x) has been used. I do not understand why! Do you have some
> intuition? Should we ask this question to Rue (since he made the
> note). Perhaps I should make a follow-up-question that is easier to
> follow, based on the note you provided.
>
> Best
>
> Fredrik

> > Yes, I believe that is correct. INLA uses 'conditioning by Kriging'
> > to correct for the constraints while retaining the sparsity of the Q
> > matrix. See section 2.3.3 of Rue and Held (and eqn 2.31 for how to
> > efficiently calculate the conditional density, which I glossed over
> > too quickly on my first **several** reads...).
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Jeff

> > sparse.

> > > Subject: [r-inla] The sparse parametrisation of the BYM-model
> > >
> > > Dear INLA users,
> > >
> > > I have a question that might be a bit technical. Any help would be
> > > appreciated.
> > >
> > > I have read the paper An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for
> > > disease mapping that accounts for scaling.
> > >
> > > I do not quite follow on the sparse-ness property of the BYM-
> > > model, which is derived in the paper. In the paper it is stated
> > > that the precision matrix of [w1,w2] is
> > >
> > >
> > > Q_tot=
> > > [ tau/(1-phi) I-matrix,-sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix ]
> > > [ -sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix, Q_*+phi/(1-phi) I-matrix ]
> > >
> > > where I is an identity-matrix.
> > >
> > > If we invert Q_tot and then consider the lower right block of
> > > this matrix, i.e. the covariance matrix for the spatial term,
> > > (call it Sigma22) and then invert this, we get Sigma_22^{-1}=Q_*,
> > > which is sparse. But have we not enforced a sum to zero constraint
> > > on w_2? Then the precision matrix should not be sparse? We should
> > > have that Sigma_22 = Q^(-1)-Q^(-1)t(A)((AQ^(-1)t(A)))^(-1)AQ^(-1)
> > > (Taken from Rues book).
> > >
> > > I have tried to illustrate the calculations using the Germany-
> > > dataset and the example used in the help-section for the function
> > > inla.scale.model.
> > >
> > > Where am I wrong?
> > >
> > > #Example start
> > > #Small number to be added to the diagonal of Q
> > >
> > > eps = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
> > >
> > > library(INLA)
> > >
> > > data(Germany)
> > >
> > > g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
> > >
> > > source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Q = -inla.graph2matrix(g)
> > >
> > > diag(Q) = 0
> > >
> > > diag(Q) = -rowSums(Q)
> > >
> > > n = dim(Q)[1]
> > >
> > > Q.scaled = inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n),
> > > e=0))
> > >
> > > Q.scaled
> > >
> > > Q.scaled.eps=Q.scaled+diag(n)*eps
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > A=matrix(1, 1, n)
> > >
> > > tau_b=0.5
> > >
> > > phi=0.5
> > >
> > > I=Matrix(0,n,n,sparse=TRUE)
> > >
> > > diag(I)=1
> > >
> > > upper=cbind(tau_b/(1-phi)*I,-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I)
> > >
> > > lower=cbind(-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I,Q.scaled.eps+phi/(1-phi)*I)
> > >
> > > Precision=rbind(upper,lower)
> > >
> > > Sigma=solve(Precision)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > #Extract the covariance matrix for the spatial term
> > >
> > > Sigma.spatial=Sigma[(n+1):(2*n),(n+1):(2*n)]
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > diag(Q.scaled.eps)-diag(solve(Sigma.spatial))
> > >
> > > #The diagonals match
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > solve(Sigma.spatial)
> > >
> > > #Which is sparse,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > #We see that the elements are the same. One example:
> > >
> > > Q.scaled.eps[544,534]
> > >
> > > solve(Sigma.spatial)[544,534]
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > #However, is w2~sim N(0,Q.scaled.eps^-1) or N(0,Q.scaled^-) where
> > > Q.scaled^- is #the generalized variance.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > #What is the sigma of the spatial term under sum to zero
> > > constraint? Expression from Rue's book.
> > >
> > > A=matrix(1, 1, n)
> > >
> > > Component1=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps))
> > >
> > > Component2=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A)%*%solve(A%*%solve(
> > > Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A))%*%A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps))
> > >
> > > Sigma.spatial.correct=Component1-Component2
> > >
> > > diag(Sigma.spatial.correct)-diag(solve(Q.scaled.eps))
> > >
> > > #These do not match, as expected.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > #Example end
> > >
> > > Best regards
> > >
> > > Fredrik
